Definition: A control that enforces network traffic policy across a trust boundary.
Intrusion Detection System -- an out-of-band monitoring technology that detects suspicious traffic but does not block it directly.
Intrusion Prevention System -- an inline control that inspects and blocks malicious traffic in real time.
Web Application Firewall -- a control that protects web applications by detecting and filtering malicious HTTP or HTTPS traffic.
An intermediary in front of users that controls and inspects their outbound requests.
A server-side intermediary that receives inbound requests on behalf of backend services.
A control point that authenticates, validates, meters, and logs API calls.
Network Access Control -- technology that evaluates endpoint identity or posture before granting network access.
A device or virtual feature that copies a link's traffic to a monitoring tool without sitting in the traffic path.
A system that gathers logs, flow records, or packet copies from many sources for central analysis.
Content Delivery Network -- a distributed edge network that caches content and absorbs attack traffic in front of origin servers.
Distributing traffic across multiple nodes, using health checks, so one failure does not stop the service.
The ability of an environment to restore business function after failure or compromise.
Increasing capacity by distributing workload across multiple systems.
Increasing capacity by adding more resources to a single system.
Keeping state over time versus frequently rebuilding or discarding systems to limit attacker dwell time.
An architectural approach that denies implicit trust based on location and instead validates access continuously.
Policy Decision Point -- the component that evaluates policy and returns an allow or deny decision.
Policy Enforcement Point -- the component in the data path that applies the PDP's decision.
An area where entities are trusted by default after an initial check.
Reevaluating whether access remains justified throughout the life of a session.
Requiring stronger proof of identity when contextual risk changes.
The precise access relationship between a requester and a protected resource.
Separating an environment into zones so a compromise in one cannot freely reach another.
Fine-grained traffic control between individual workloads, services, or applications.
A VPN that connects automatically whenever a managed device is online.
Moving away from sole reliance on a single network perimeter as the primary trust model.
Secure Access Service Edge -- a cloud-delivered architecture that pairs SD-WAN with security services (SSE) near the user and workload.
Zero Trust Network Access -- brokered, per-application access that replaces broad VPN access to the network.
Software-Defined Wide Area Network -- policy-driven path selection and security across sites, cloud, and branches.
Software-Defined Networking -- separating the control plane from the data plane so network policy is set in software.
Evidence that a device or workload is in a trustworthy state.
A segment that holds high-value assets behind tightly controlled entry points.
Guardrails that keep data within trusted identities, devices, networks, and destinations.
Continuously identifying and reducing externally reachable systems and exposures.
Removing unnecessary functionality and insecure defaults from a system.
Layering controls so that the failure of one safeguard does not automatically produce compromise.
Collecting identity, network, endpoint, and cloud events in one place for correlation and investigation.
Proactively searching retained telemetry for attacker activity that no alert has raised.
A scheme of sensitivity categories that determines how data must be handled.
Marking data with visible or machine-readable indicators of sensitivity or handling requirements.
Applying metadata to resources or data so that automated controls can enforce policy.
Data Loss Prevention -- a set of controls designed to prevent sensitive data from being lost, exposed, or exfiltrated.
Continuous scanning of repositories to find sensitive data the organization did not know it had.
Evidence from assessments, scanning, and metrics that a control actually reduces risk.
